meta.title: Nathalie González Pérez
meta.description: Registered Behavior Technician transitioning into UX design and AI for social impact.

hero.subtitle: Certified behavior technician (RBT) transitioning into UX design and AI applied to social impact.

about.heading: One question, three different doors.
paragraphs: I was studying medicine in Cuba, at the University of Medical Sciences in Pinar del Río — near the top of my class, with a clear path ahead. Circumstances at home forced me to leave before finishing: two years done, a plan interrupted.

I arrived in the United States without fluent English. I waited tables while teaching myself the language. I earned my Registered Behavior Technician (RBT) certification while still working — and found a new door back to the same calling: helping people function and be understood.

Leaving medicine didn't mean leaving the reason I wanted to be a doctor. I've kept following that same pattern — not waiting for the right degree or the right permission, I've been teaching myself UX design and AI and applying it to real projects. Self-taught English, then RBT certification while waiting tables, and now UX and AI on my own while working as an RBT. The same mission, rebuilt.

hero.title: Leaf
hero.tagline: Care for your plants without guessing when to water them.

problem.heading: A visual and functional language for daily care.
problem.body: Leaf was born as the capstone for my Google UX Design Certificate: an app that helps indoor-plant owners organize watering, light, and general-care reminders. The challenge wasn't technical — it was finding the right tone: useful without being controlling, calm without being boring.

research.heading: I started by listening.
research.body: I designed personas, ran a competitive audit, defined the value proposition, and framed 'How Might We…' questions and goal statements. Research surfaced two common failure modes across the category: asking users for too much upfront, or turning plant care into an anxious to-do list. Leaf had to do the opposite.
bullets: Personas grounded in real user interviews.
Competitive audit across 5 apps in the category.
Prioritized value proposition and 'How Might We…' questions.
Goal statements to scope the MVP.

process.heading: From wireframes to a design system.
process.body: I designed low-fidelity wireframes first, iterating on feedback before touching color or typography. The design system (palette, typography, components) grew as a reusable library — every ReminderCard, button, and bottom-sheet overlay lives as a component in Figma. The app was prototyped in high fidelity and moved to production with Claude Code via MCP.

results.heading: Real usability study.
results.body: I ran a study with 5 participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The final score was 76 — above the industry average (68), in the 'good' range. What mattered more than the number was what the study surfaced.
learnings: Users wanted to see at a glance which plant needed attention today — I redesigned the home to prioritize 'next care' over full inventory.
Onboarding asked for too much upfront — I broke it into progressive steps with an option to defer detail.
Reminder copy worked better concise and warm-toned, not like a system notification.

reflection.heading: What I take away.
reflection.body: A good design system isn't about having many components — it's about having the right ones and using them consistently. And user research doesn't stop when design starts; it comes back to you on every iteration. If I started over, I'd invest more time in the usability study and less in polishing mockups before testing them.

hero.title: Cata
hero.tagline: A personal wine journal with a pairing assistant.

problem.heading: A wine journal as an intimate space, not a database.
problem.body: Existing wine apps treat every bottle as a catalog entry — rating, notes, photo. Cata starts from a different question: what story does this bottle tell inside your life? A personal journal that also helps you decide what to eat with what you've got.

research.heading: Scoping it.
research.body: As a personal project, research was lighter and direct: sessions with wine-loving friends to understand what they log today (spoiler: nothing consistent) and which moments they actually want to remember. The takeaway: the barrier isn't a lack of apps, it's the friction of opening them.

process.heading: Design and build, in the same session.
process.body: I designed the full system in Figma — palette, typography, component library — and used Claude Code via MCP to move it into production directly from the mockups. The workflow shortened the design→code cycle dramatically: every UI iteration could be tested in the browser the same day.
flows: Detail view with notes and context

results.heading: In build, with focus.
results.body: Cata is under active development. Instead of chasing features, I'm prioritizing that logging a bottle feels like writing a postcard — quick, personal, frictionless. The current version covers the full capture and detail flow; the pairing assistant lands in the next iteration.
learnings: Initial input should be photo-first — most users don't want to type before they have visual context.
The pairing assistant works better as a contextual suggestion inside the bottle detail, not as a separate screen.
Designing the system upfront let Claude Code generate consistent UI without rework.

reflection.heading: What I take away.
reflection.body: Cata taught me that designing and building in the same flow changes how you make decisions — you test ideas before you commit to them. The design system isn't the final deliverable; it's the infrastructure that lets you iterate fast without losing coherence.
